These were combined to analyze how regional level biofuel supply compares to demand and potential impact on fuel adoption. The analysis uses the U.S. Census Bureau’s four regions—Northeast, Midwest, South, and West—each with the following divisions: Northeast (New England, Middle Atlantic); Midwest (East North Central, West North Central); South (South Atlantic, East South Central, West South Central); and West (Mountain, Pacific) (U.S. Census Bureau, 2025). 5.3.1 Results Figures 5-15 and 5-16 compare regional RD and BD production from the BILT model’s baseline scenario—50‑mile facility spacing and unstacked siting against projected 2035 rail diesel demand. These figures represent RD100 and BD100 cases. Note that for HEFA and transesterification pathways, the figures show cases if soybean is used to produce either RD or BD, but not both simultaneously. As noted in Section 3.1, BILT was run separately for each pathway; there is no competition across pathways for feedstock or siting. Figure 5-15 Regional Biofuel Production and Rail Energy Demand for 100% Renewable Diesel Scenario in 2035 (Other Feedstocks that are not Accounted for in this Study could Add Additional Volume Beyond what is Reported Here) In Figure 5-15, RD from soybean HEFA shows substantial scale-up potential, indicating a near- term opportunity for the rail sector and making HEFA the dominant RD pathway. RD from soybean-HEFA accounts for 85% of total RD production, 10% from woody-gasification and FT- 52 synthesis and 5% from manure and sludge HTL. Total RD production is sufficient to meet all rail diesel demand in 2035 and to supply an additional 11% of diesel demand in other sectors. Likewise, in the BD100 case, the remaining BD could supply 8.5% of diesel demand in other sectors. Figure 5-16 Regional Biofuel Production and Rail Energy Demand for 100% Biodiesel Scenario in 2035 RD and/or BD production from soybean and waste feedstocks provides near-term opportunities while woody and herbaceous biomass provides long-term opportunities. RD-HEFA and BD- transesterification from soybeans are mature technologies and they are commercialized pathways with high fuel yield per ton of feedstock. For woody biomass pathways considered in this study, availability of woody biomass for processing limits RD production. These woody pathways require a 50/50 blend of feedstock, so the unused residues and unused trees are often not in places that can be moved to a central location for processing (Section 3.1). In addition, the volume of fuel produced per ton of woody biomass is lower compared to biofuel quantity using first-generation feedstock such as corn or soybean. The low availability of wet wastes limit RD scalability from HTL. Alternative fuel selection for the rail sector can start with RD in the near term at lower cost. Note that soybean quantity adopted in this study accounts only for the soybeans that are currently used for fuel production and not for food.
